title: Scaling Limits of Long-Context Transformers
claim: A single scaling parameter splits behavior into regimes, with error shrinking, bottoming out, then plateauing at a critical threshold where selectivity emerges.
layout: 1 plot with shaded regime bands, three inset bar charts, left-to-right axis
description: A single large plot has the inverse temperature β_n on the x-axis and the expected error E||Y_n(q)|| on the y-axis. The background is split into shaded vertical bands: light blue for the two subcritical regimes, a thick gray line for the critical point, and pale orange for the supercritical regime. A blue curve falls like β_n^{-1}, turns gray after a first minimum at n^{2/(d+1)}, and rises as n^{-1/2}β_n^{(d-3)/4} to the critical point at n^{2/(d-1)}. Past that point the curve is a flat orange line. Dashed guides mark the axis values. Three white inset panels show bar charts of ordered attention weights A_(i). They are nearly uniform in the subcritical regime, decaying at criticality, and a single spike in the supercritical regime. Bold regime labels sit along the top. The bottom of the plot is labeled 'drift ≫ fluctuation' and 'fluctuation ≫ drift'.

abstract: We study the long-context limit of softmax self-attention with a fixed query and a random context of $n$ i.i.d. keys on the sphere with the intrinsic dimension of the key distribution held fixed, viewing the inverse temperature $Î²_n$ as the scaling parameter that decides whether attention degenerates into uniform averaging or collapses onto the single closest key. We show that the critical scale at which selectivity emerges is determined by the local exponent of the distance-to-query distribution near zero rather than by global features of the context, and scales like $Î²_n^\ast \asymp n^{2/(d-1)}$ for uniform keys on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Furthermore, we characterize the limiting laws of the ordered attention weights and of the attention output across all regimes of $Î²_n$: a subcritical regime in which the output reduces to a local average around $q$ with explicit deterministic bias and Gaussian fluctuations; a critical regime in which a finite collection of nearest keys retains macroscopic mass without single-key collapse; and a supercritical regime in which all mass concentrates on the closest key. Of notable interest is the subcritical case with identity value matrix where the attention map approximately implements a backward heat equation.
